title: Can you structure these 8 investment case questions in two minutes each?
description: 8 investment case prompts to structure in two minutes each, with model answers, where to start and the trap to avoid.
hook: Investment prompts come down to need, payback and alternatives. Watch for the ones where squeezing existing capacity beats building new. Give yourself two minutes per prompt, then open the model and look for what you missed.
body:
1. Should a car maker build its own battery plant?

Show a model structure
  • Need: Our battery demand and supply security; Prices and lead times from suppliers
  • Make vs buy economics: Plant cost vs buying, per kWh; Payback and NPV
  • Risks: Technology changing fast; Can we run a plant at scale?
  • Alternatives: Joint venture, long-term supply contracts; Buying a stake in a supplier

Where to start: Make vs buy cost per kWh over the life of the plant.

The trap: Ignoring that battery technology may change before the plant pays back.

2. Should a supermarket open dark stores for 15-minute delivery?

Show a model structure
  • Demand: How many orders per dark store per day; Density: orders within a 15-minute radius
  • Economics per order: Basket size, delivery fee; Picking, delivery, rent per order
  • Cannibalisation: Orders taken from our own stores and online; Net new profit
  • Competition and operations: Rapid-delivery rivals burning cash; Can we staff and stock it?

Where to start: Economics per order: rapid delivery usually loses money on every order at low volume.

The trap: Assuming every order is new and not taken from our own stores.

3. Should a UK university open a campus in Singapore?

Show a model structure
  • Demand: Students in the region and their willingness to pay; Competition from local and other foreign universities
  • Economics: Set-up cost, fees, staff; Break-even student numbers
  • Quality and brand: Teaching and degrees equal to home; Risk to reputation
  • Regulation and partners: Local approvals; Partner or go alone

Where to start: Demand: will enough students pay close to UK fees in Singapore?

The trap: Assuming home demand carries over to a new market.

4. Should a delivery company switch its 2,000 vans to electric?

Show a model structure
  • Cost per mile: Van price, energy, maintenance; Resale value and grants
  • Operations: Range vs daily routes; Charging at depots, time to charge
  • Investment and timing: Upfront cost, financing; Switch all now vs as vans retire
  • Other benefits and risks: Clean-air zones, customer demands; Battery life, grid capacity

Where to start: Total cost per mile over a van's life, not the purchase price.

The trap: Comparing only purchase prices.

5. Should a fashion retailer launch a loyalty programme?

Show a model structure
  • Customer behaviour: Would members visit and spend more?; Share of sales from repeat customers
  • Costs: Rewards given, app, marketing; Rewards to customers who would buy anyway
  • Data value: Personalised offers; Better buying and pricing
  • Competition: Rivals' programmes; What makes ours different

Where to start: Rewards to customers who would buy anyway: the hidden cost of loyalty schemes.

The trap: Counting all member spending as extra.

6. Should an online retailer build its own warehouse or keep using a third-party one?

Show a model structure
  • Cost per order: Our cost at scale vs the third party's fees; Volume needed to beat them
  • Investment: Building, automation, payback; Flexibility if volumes change
  • Service: Delivery speed, errors; Control over the customer experience
  • Capability and risk: Can we run a warehouse well?; Peak season

Where to start: Volume needed for our cost per order to beat the third party's fee.

The trap: Comparing costs at today's volume instead of planned volume.

7. Should a hospital buy a $2M surgical robot?

Show a model structure
  • Clinical benefit: Outcomes, recovery time; Which operations use it
  • Economics: Cost per operation, consumables; Extra patients, shorter stays
  • Capacity: Surgeons trained, theatre time; Operations per year needed
  • Alternatives: Share with another hospital; Lease instead of buy

Where to start: Operations per year needed to make it worthwhile.

The trap: Buying for prestige without enough cases to use it.

8. Should a government back a new nuclear power station?

Show a model structure
  • Need: Electricity demand, other low-carbon options; Energy security
  • Cost: Build cost, overruns, cost per MWh; Who pays: taxpayers or bill payers
  • Risk: Delays, safety, waste; Financing over decades
  • Alternatives: Wind, solar plus storage, gas with capture; Small modular reactors

Where to start: Cost per MWh vs the alternatives, including the risk of overruns.

The trap: Comparing the build cost without the risk of delays.
